summary: Reviews how roaming systems were designed and built in 1997, where a user of one network provider can dial in through another. Examples include groups of internet providers sharing access and companies letting staff connect from elsewhere. It is an informational survey rather than a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo surveys systems that let a user dial in through a local provider while keeping an account with a home provider. It compares how the systems found access numbers, checked users, assigned network settings and recorded usage in 1997.

subtitle: A survey of how dial-up users accessed service through another provider in 1997.

tldr.problem: A user may want to access the Internet through a local provider while keeping an account with a different home provider, requiring coordination across networks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reviews several roaming systems and compares their phone directories, authentication, network access, address assignment, security and accounting arrangements.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2194 is an Informational survey of implementations and trade-offs as they stood in 1997, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 2194 is an Informational survey published in September 1997, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the roaming implementations and their status at that time.

sections.title: What Roaming Requires
sections.content:
The memo defines roaming as using one of several Internet service providers while maintaining a customer relationship with only one. The home ISP holds the user's account; the local ISP is the provider the user calls for access. The memo includes ISP partnerships and corporate access among the situations where roaming may be useful.

It reviews systems against requirements such as presenting and updating access numbers, managing connections, authenticating users, configuring network access servers, assigning addresses, providing security and accounting for use. It also covers shared-use networks and non-IP dial-up networks that address some of these needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Roaming lets a customer use a local provider while keeping an account with a home provider. Both providers need ways to identify the user, arrange access and record the session.

sections.title: Authentication Across Providers
sections.content:
Several systems route a login to the user's home provider. In the GRIC example, a login such as liu@Aimnet.com identifies a domain; a routing server finds the home provider's authentication server, which accepts or rejects the credentials. The local network access server then grants access and assigns an address if authentication succeeds.

The memo also describes i-Pass, ChinaNet and Microsoft systems using forms such as username@auth_domain or username@realm with RADIUS proxies. ChinaNet can cache successful user information for three days by default. The Microsoft implementation also supports a prefix login form for devices with shorter user ID limits. MichNet uses realms and RADIUS core servers to forward requests to participating organizations' authentication servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The local provider can forward a login request to the system that holds the user's account. The home system checks the credentials and sends the result back through the local provider.

sections.title: Access Numbers and Phone Books
sections.content:
The implementations distribute access numbers in different ways. GRIC compiled member numbers into phone books available through a web directory or client. i-Pass maintained an access-point database that users could search or download. ChinaNet used a nationwide access number in the described system and did not then require a phone book.

Microsoft's system used phone-book files that could be updated with difference files, while FidoNet distributed weekly changes to its Nodelist. The memo notes that FidoNet used the list to map system addresses to phone numbers, but did not provide IP service or distributed user authentication, so users could not roam between systems in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Each system needed a way for users to find local access numbers and keep the list current. Some systems downloaded updates; FidoNet sent changes to a shared list of dial-up systems.

sections.title: Different Network Settings Can Conflict
sections.content:
A home provider may return network settings that do not fit the local network access server. The memo lists IP address, route, filter, vendor-specific and timeout attributes as possible sources of conflict. A proxy may need to edit or replace some attributes, but filter definitions and vendor-specific settings can be difficult to translate between different equipment.

The memo points out that RADIUS does not distinguish mandatory from optional attributes, so a proxy cannot always know whether an attribute can safely be removed. It also notes that static configuration files can become tedious as a roaming group grows; it discusses DNS SRV records as a possible way to map a domain to a RADIUS server.
sections.plainLanguage: The home provider's network settings may not work on the local provider's equipment. A proxy may need to adjust settings, but the memo says some differences are hard to resolve safely.

sections.title: Security, Accounting and the Survey's Scope
sections.content:
The reviewed systems used different security approaches. The memo describes password hashing between GRIC authentication servers, encryption and certificates in i-Pass, and encryption between ChinaNet RADIUS servers. It notes that the Microsoft RADIUS proxy did not support token cards or tunneling protocols at the time, and that FidoNet coordinator submissions lacked security protection against fraudulent updates.

Accounting also differed: central services or providers collected session records and used them for settlement or billing. The RFC reports that MichNet had 4,774 dial-in lines on May 1, 1997. RFC 2194 is a survey of these systems, not a common protocol or current status report.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementations differed in how they protected credentials and transferred accounting records. This memo records those design choices as a survey, rather than defining one shared roaming protocol.
